AI-Defined Vehicles Push Compute, Memory, And Validation Limits

5

Shares

4

The shift from software-defined to AI-defined vehicles raises questions about whether the hardware can keep up.

October 1st, 2026 -

By: Brendan Heffernan

Key Takeaways:

Automakers are making different bets on compute architecture, with some favoring large central processors while others distribute specialized compute across AI-defined vehicle systems.
Moving sensor data is becoming as important as processing it, with raw camera and radar data putting new demands on memory, interfaces, in-vehicle networks, and power efficiency.
AI-defined vehicle systems must verify sensor inputs, AI decisions, and updates across edge cases and over a vehicle’s long service life.

Carmakers are racing to develop and incorporate advanced AI capabilities into vehicles in order to capitalize on what is expected to be a $1 trillion-plus market for physical AI over the next decade.
To be competitive in this market, automakers will need to upgrade today’s software-defined vehicle systems to automotive electronics frameworks that can efficiently handle the memory, compute, and power demands in these systems.
“A software-defined vehicle is one whose functionality evolves through software updates after it leaves the factory, but an AI-defined vehicle goes a step further, using AI to continuously interpret data, make decisions, and adapt behavior in real time,” said Paul Karazuba, vice president of product marketing for Silicon IP at Rambus. “The difference is not just software that changes, but intelligence that actively shapes how the vehicle operates.”
But effectively leveraging that intelligence requires rethinking the automobile’s basic architecture, the supply chain for parts and data, and the methodology for creating, integrating, testing, and monitoring adaptable complex systems of systems under harsh ambient conditions.
“AI is not a value proposition in itself, but an essential enabling technology for the continued evolution of SDVs and AI-defined vehicles,” said Moritz Neukirchner, senior director of cross-portfolio growth and strategic alliances, Elektrobit. “AI has been part of vehicles for many years — in perception stacks for advanced driver assistance systems, for example. What changes with the AIDV is the experience. Functionality becomes visible and directly accessible to customers, while AI accelerators and development capabilities become more accessible to software developers. The first customer-facing applications naturally center on speech assistants and conversational interfaces. At the same time, the evolving developer experience is enabling less visible but equally important applications, including AI-assisted remote diagnostics and observability solutions that help monitor, understand, and maintain vehicle software throughout its lifecycle.”
Enabling this transition will provide semiconductor companies with several enhanced revenue streams. “The transition to the so-called ‘AI-defined’ vehicles can be seen as the next generation of software-defined vehicles,” said Paula Jones, senior director of automotive at Infineon. “Currently, traditional OEMs are working toward SDVs, where software defines key features, built on hardware building blocks of zone control modules, central compute, and standard communication along with AI features and over-the-air updates. This is a good opportunity for semiconductor companies like Infineon to provide the critical hardware and software elements, including automotive-qualified microcontrollers, Ethernet, and sensors to drive this upcoming generation of SDVs, defined by AI.”
Exactly how system designers will enable those advancements is not yet defined, and different OEMs are approaching the same problems differently.
Betting on compute architecture
One of the biggest questions facing the developing ecosystem hinges on how centralized a vehicle’s compute architecture should be. OEMs usually choose one of two approaches to compute architecture — a more centralized, compute-power-first solution with larger chips, or more distributed “right-sized” architecture.
“Different OEMs are making different bets,” said Michal Siwinski, executive vice president, chief product and marketing officer, and general manager for security solutions at Arteris. “It will be interesting to see what ends up happening a few years down the line. You want to make sure these things are in production deployment for years, not for months. We will know in a few years whether both approaches are equal. Right now, it’s too early to tell. There is a bit of a tug-of-war going on.”
Both approaches have their pros and cons. “The ‘server-on-wheels’ is basically going for max compute. It’s all about throughput, performance, and maximizing your power envelope,” said Siwinski. “The more compute you have, the better the mindset. It’s a bit of a brute force approach, but you can have that. You build these amazing super chips. You put a bunch of them in the car, and they can be the central compute for everything. Let’s say you’re building something you want to be very safe and very secure. At the same time, it is a single point of failure. If you take more of a distributed architecture, it’s different. You can have a more best-in-class solution, and you’re not doing one-size-fits-all compute because you can optimize. This chip says it’s going to be doing this for that application, and you have more of a pick-your-best. So it’s kind of the classical situation where you ask if it is better to have built one thing that does everything or have something that’s more purpose-built?”
The AI-defined vehicle push has designers experimenting with a variety of chip architecture solutions. “One of the additional problems is people are using GPUs for more and more things that they haven’t used GPUs for in the past,” said Rob Fisher, director of product management at Imagination Technologies. “Whereas they might have used an NPU to do AI processing previously, they may now look at the GPU as an excellent way to do AI processing. This isn’t typically done today, so we have a whole new realm of possibilities that we need to consider.”
Chiplets also offer some intriguing possibilities for AI-defined vehicles. “We have a vision at Cadence that chiplets will be a new way of delivering technology, and one of the reasons is that you can make chips application-specific, and we are now making systems that are getting much more complex, with AI at the edge everywhere,” said Sylvain Guilley, chief technology officer at Secure-IC, a Cadence company. “This means, in any robot or car, you will have the same need for compute, the same need for AI inference and even safety functions, at different locations. It’s much more economical to use the same chiplets across the full system. Chiplets are going to play an important role because we are redefining autonomous systems that have many different sensors.”
Data and memory bottlenecks
When designing these AI-defined vehicle systems, figuring out the most efficient way to move sensor and communications data is as important as figuring out what to process it with.
“AI workloads are generating more data than ever, and feeding processors efficiently is becoming just as important as the compute itself,” said Rambus’ Karazuba. “The biggest bottlenecks are data movement, power efficiency, and system trust. Feeding processors efficiently is becoming just as important as the compute itself. At the same time, automotive systems must deliver that performance while meeting strict safety, security, and reliability requirements over a vehicle’s lifetime.”
With AI sensors constantly pulling in new data, the key challenge is finding more powerful solutions that work at a practical cost. “The point cloud is a lot more data to move to a central processing unit that is much more powerful than what we see in classic and traditional ECUs. How do we get the data there?” said Sven Kopacz, autonomous vehicle section manager at Keysight Technologies. “Just think of a rear camera. You put the vehicle in reverse, you want the picture on your screen, so you need to tell the camera that you’re on now. So that’s what, 20 bytes? It’s a small message you want to send in that direction. But now you have the camera stream coming in this direction. This is an asymmetric connection, and we cover it with what we call SerDes, which is optimized for asymmetric use cases. In a car, if you can save 10 cents on a module, you will go for that. Same for the wiring. We also see the automotive OEMs moving to optical now, because if you go with Ethernet and you want to wire up every peer with another one, you end up with a lot of extra wiring.”
These new workload demands are also pushing automotive OEMs to rethink who they trust to support their data processing. “We have a lot more data to process in the car, and also to transport,” said Kopacz. “Now OEMs are moving toward a point where they say, ‘We want to differentiate on how we process that data. We just don’t want to rely on a black box, so we want that point cloud. I don’t want you to do the processing. A Tier One might sell this processing module to an OEM. It could come out of the same source, but the OEM wants the flexibility to choose how they want to combine that, and they may put much more trust into a new player in the ecosystem, let’s say Nvidia, that is familiar with how to process a point cloud and do object recognition.”
AI-defined vehicle systems also must verify sensor inputs, AI decisions, and updates across edge cases and over a vehicle’s long service life.
“If you’re driving a car around for 20 years maybe, the technology that launches Day One has to stay out there, and these AIs aren’t used to that,” said Carrie Browen, autonomous vehicle business line manager at Keysight Technologies. “The AI that you and I use regularly is constantly learning and changing, but in the car it must do it right. That’s a different kind of learning: to come back, validate that decision, and validate that the loop is correct. That’s the other end of it. The data must go all the way through. It must come from the collection into the car, and then you must prove and ensure the safety of the people that are relying on those decisions are being made because of that data.”
The reality of these data and verification requirements also underscores the growing memory bottleneck in AV development. “What tends to matter is our ability to move the bytes, store the bytes in order to enable efficient operation,” said Rahul Rithe, director of autonomy sensing systems at Rivian, at this month’s JEDEC Automotive Electronics Forum. “To get the incremental improvement in performance, it requires an exponential increase in the compute and also in the memory, and this is really the key bottleneck that we are now running into. The memory bandwidth and capacity are the gating resources for advanced autonomy and physical AI.”
Automotive component lifecycles in the AI-defined vehicle era
With automotive chips expected to last much longer than their counterparts in other sectors, like data centers, OEMs already are making vehicle AI architecture decisions based on maximizing lifespan. “An example of a decision that industry is making is this shift to potentially Automotive Ethernet and Optical Automotive Ethernet in the inner vehicle connectivity,” said Browen. “That way they can get rid of some of the nodes that are another physical thing that has a certain number of relays, or a certain number of switches that are associated with it. So by switching to Ethernet on that backplane, but also switching to Ethernet for those edge devices — for the devices like your seat control and your power windows, or all the little ECUs that are in the car, if that can all be on one IP, one network — you can get rid of these extra nodes. It’s a decision the industry is making to remove some of those physical components in the car for longevity reasons.”
Keeping AI-powered vehicles on the road longer gives OEMs an extra incentive to sell software upgrades. “OEMs are talking about even longer lifespans for the platform, because for SDVs, a future revenue stream would be selling upgrades through plain software upgrades enabling features,” Kopacz said. “They want to keep the platform alive a little longer.”
Conclusion
The shift to AI-defined vehicles will be measured less by how much AI an automaker can put in a car than by how reliably the entire system works over its lifespan.
As software and models evolve after production, automakers also will need to preserve the evidence that each update behaves safely across vehicle variants and years of use. The architecture that succeeds will be the one OEMs can best deploy, validate, maintain, and afford at scale.
That long-term support begins during development, but it also needs to be extensible. AI-assisted engineering could accelerate delivery, but its outputs must remain traceable and reproducible.
“AI is driving a step change in how automotive software is designed, implemented, tested, integrated and qualified,” said Elektrobit’s Neukirchner. “This has the potential to shorten development cycles, improve engineering productivity, and make the complexity of SDV development more manageable. This depends on the resulting software and evidence remaining traceable, reproducible, and governed throughout the lifecycle. It is equally important not to repeat a common mistake in SDV programs — treating the ease of greenfield development as a reason to rebuild everything. The greater challenge is reusing existing assets to ensure commercial viability while enabling controlled evolution across vehicle platforms, variants, model years,  and generations. This continuity is essential to make AIDV development economically sustainable at scale.”
